sections.heading: Where this sits for you
body: **19 of the official questions in Area and volume are this one** — 2 Easy, 9 Medium, 8 Hard.
It is top-heavy: most versions are Hard, so it only earns study time once your target actually requires that tier.

sections.heading: How to spot it
body: You are looking at this pattern when:
- The question names a solid (rectangular prism, cylinder, cone, pyramid, sphere or hemisphere) and gives its dimensions, sometimes on a labelled figure.
- Choices often leave π in the answer, or the question asks for the value next to π.

sections.heading: The method
body: - 1) Look up the formula on the reference sheet.
- Cones and pyramids get ⅓, a sphere is (4/3)πr³, and a hemisphere is half of that.
- 2) Before substituting, turn a diameter into a radius and apply any percent change to the dimension.
- 3) Substitute and simplify, leaving π in if the choices keep it.

sections.heading: Where Desmos fits
body: Type the formula with the numbers substituted, for example (1/3)π r² h with r and h filled in, and compare the result to the choices.
If the choices have π in them, divide your result by π.

sections.heading: What it is built to catch
body: The question gives you a diameter so that you will use it as the radius, which makes the answer 4 times too big.
You may also forget the ⅓ for a cone or pyramid, or the ½ for a hemisphere.
When a dimension is scaled by a percent, you may apply the percent to the volume instead of to the radius.

sections.heading: You are losing these
body: Before you choose, say out loud what the question is asking for — not what you solved for.
The question gives you a diameter so that you will use it as the radius, which makes the answer 4 times too big.
You may also forget the ⅓ for a cone or pyramid, or the ½ for a hemisphere.
